newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic's Serbia crisis strategy takes shape.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic's Serbia crisis strategy takes shape.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic's strategy to defuse an election-rigging crisis in Serbia that has sapped his grip on power is slowly taking shape, political sources said on Wednesday.
A month of street demonstrations by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition has convinced Milosevic he can no longer avoid concessions to head off a wider threat to his rule.
Western diplomats believed he was weighing whether to admit Zajedno won Belgrade and 14 of Serbia's biggest towns in local elections on November 17, or offer fresh elections.
Neither solution contained comfort for his ruling socialists who face ceding power to their political foes after half a century of unbroken power.
Either could bring about a sea change in Serbia's political life by spurring democratic reforms that would break the back of effective one-party rule.
Surrendering the capital and other towns to Zajedno would give the opposition a high-profile platform to promote themselves as an alternative to socialism.
But political sources said this option might be preferable to fresh elections which threaten greater risks.
Zajedno would certainly insist on international monitoring to guarantee a new vote was fair. In Serbia's present mood, the socialists might suffer an even worse defeat.
Importantly, Zajedno would demand that Milosevic give up the stranglehold on Serbia's national media which buttresses his power.

The sources said his first gambit would probably be to acknowledge the election results, knowing that the socialists still in authority nationally would not lack opportunities to make opposition mayors look like bungling amateurs.
Courts have already ordered the socialists to hand back two towns which Zajedno won including Nis, an industrial powerhouse and Serbia's second largest city.
In a further sign, Milosevic on Tuesday accepted documents from Nis students which they claimed were proof of election fraud by the local socialists.
He sent the papers to justice ministry for investigation with a promise to the students that the law would be upheld.

Political sources said that even at this late stage in the conflict, the Serbian leader was positioning himself to claim he was unaware of socialist misdemeanours ahead of a visit by a delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
He invited the OSCE team, led by Spain's former socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzales, to verify the election results after a U.S.-led outcry in the west in support of Zajedno.
The opposition, now being intensively advised by the United States, is showing more realism in its demands.

Utopian calls for Milosevic's resignation are rarer. The opposition campaign is focused on getting the election result honoured in preparation for an attempt to defeat the socialists in Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections in 1997.
Opposition leader Miroljub Labus said after talks with U.S. officials and congressmen that Zajedno would get full American support "if it introduced democracy into Serbia in a democratic way."
Washington was also telling Zajedno that a democratised Serbia would be rewarded with the help it needs to rebuild its shattered economy.
Without access to the media, it is almost impossible for the opposition to reach beyond its urban powerbase and try to convert Milosevic's bedrock in the provinces with this message.
The pensioners, farmers and workers who keep the socialists in power have seen only state television's portrayal of Zajedno supporters as terrorists and wreckers.
This conservative constituency is easily manipulated and has been taught to be suspicious of the West's motives in Serbia after its isolation under U.N. sanctions during the war in Bosnia.
Milosevic warned the Nis students on Tuesday about Zajedno's alliances with Washington and western European governments.
"However much your leaders go to embassies and send envoys and travel to world capitals, a foreign hand shall not rule Serbia," he said. "We are our own masters in Serbia."
